# rotating Jones vectors: U(2), SU(2), and the Poincaré sphere

{{< iconify lucide construction >}} this page is under construction {{< iconify lucide construction >}}

Having written polarization states as Jones vectors in [the previous chapter](jones_vectors.qmd),
the natural next question is: what matrices are allowed to act on them? Physically, a
wave plate rotates one polarization into another by delaying the vertical component
relative to the horizontal one by some phase. Mathematically, I want to find the group of
matrices that can represent *all* physically realizable polarization changes, and
understand why it has to be $SU(2)$ rather than something bigger or smaller.

## borrowing the logic from real rotations

Before touching complex vectors, it's worth re-deriving the familiar case: what matrices
$R$ preserve the length of a real 3D vector $v$? Length-squared is $v^\top v$, and
requiring $(Rv)^\top(Rv) = v^\top v$ for *every* $v$ forces

$$
R^\top R = I.
$$

These are the orthogonal matrices, $O(3)$. Taking determinants of both sides gives
$(\det R)^2 = 1$, so $\det R = \pm 1$: reflections get a $-1$, rotations get a $+1$.
Restricting to $\det R = +1$ is what "special" means, and that's $SO(3)$.

## the same logic, with complex entries

A Jones vector has complex entries, so "length" has to mean $\mathbf{J}^\dagger\mathbf{J}$
(Hermitian conjugate, not plain transpose) or I'd get a complex number out of a thing
that's supposed to be a probability-like intensity. Demanding that a matrix $U$ preserve
this quantity for every $\mathbf{J}$ gives, by the identical argument as above,

$$
U^\dagger U = I,
$$

the defining property of a **unitary** matrix. The $2\times2$ unitary matrices form the
group $U(2)$. Taking the determinant of $U^\dagger U = I$ gives $|\det U|^2 = 1$, so
$\det U$ is not forced to be $\pm1$ this time — it can be *any* unit-modulus complex
number $e^{i\theta}$.

This is the first place where the complex case genuinely differs from the real one, and
it matters: a generic $U(2)$ matrix carries an unavoidable overall phase in its
determinant. But I already know from the previous chapter that overall phase is
physically invisible for Jones vectors. So $U(2)$ has redundancy built into it — many
different $U(2)$ matrices produce the *same* physical rotation of the polarization
ellipse, differing only by a phase that gets thrown away anyway.

## picking a unique representative: SU(2)

To remove the redundancy, I can always rescale any $U \in U(2)$ by $e^{-i\theta/2}$
(where $\theta = \arg\det U$) to force its determinant to be exactly $1$, without
changing the physical transformation it represents. The matrices with

$$
U^\dagger U = I, \qquad \det U = 1
$$

form $SU(2)$, and this is the group that acts on Jones vectors (and, as the next chapter
shows, on quantum spin states) without any leftover ambiguity beyond the one we already
knew about and chose to ignore.

## the angle-doubling, finally made precise

Here's the calculation that I think earns the name "spinor." Physically, $H$ and $V$
polarizations are $90°$ apart in real space. But a half-wave plate — the device that
swaps $H \leftrightarrow V$ — corresponds to a *full* $180°$ rotation of the Jones vector
on the Poincaré sphere (it has to go $H \to D \to V$, a half-circle). Chasing this
through:

$$
\text{physical angle } \theta \;\longleftrightarrow\; \text{Poincaré-sphere angle } 2\theta.
$$

This is why the $SU(2)$ matrices that implement wave-plate rotations are conventionally
written with *half-angles*:

$$
U(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\theta/2} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{i\theta/2} \end{pmatrix}
$$

for rotation about the $H/V$ axis, and structurally similar matrices (built from Pauli
matrices, which will show up again when we get to Lie algebras) for rotations about the
other two axes of the sphere.

The thing I want to hold onto from this chapter is *where the factor of two actually
comes from*. It isn't some mysterious property bolted onto spinors by fiat — it falls
straight out of the fact that $(-1)\cdot\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ are the same
physical state. A rotation that looks like "half a turn" on the sphere of physical
polarization ellipses is a "full turn" on the sphere of Jones-vector directions, because
the latter sphere has already glued antipodal points together. Once you see the gluing,
the factor of two stops being surprising.
